q: Which is NOT one of the four metric properties?
w: d(a, b) ≤ d(a, c) + d(c, b) (triangle inequality)
e: The four are non-negativity, identity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.

q: A distance satisfying non-negativity, symmetry and triangle inequality, but NOT necessarily identity (M2), is a:
e: A quasimetric drops symmetry (M3) instead.

q: A distance satisfying M1, M2 and M4 but not necessarily symmetry is a:
e: Example: a one-way street network, where a→b ≠ b→a.

q: Which Lp distance is the only one invariant to rotation of the coordinate system?
e: L2 is the 'straight-line' distance and is often the default.

q: The L1 distance is also called:
e: Manhattan distance (or, in this class, the 'SLC distance'). It's the sum of |aᵢ − bᵢ|, like walking city blocks.

q: L0 distance on 0/1 vectors is known as:
e: L0 counts the coordinates where a and b differ. It isn't convex.

q: The L∞ distance between a and b is:
e: maxᵢ |aᵢ − bᵢ|: the largest deviation in any one coordinate. Geometrically it's a rotation of L1, so L1 algorithms can often be adapted to it.

q: Comparing the unit balls in ℝ²: as p gets smaller...
w: All unit balls are the same circle
The ball turns into a square
e: The unit ball gets smaller (and for p < 1 it's not convex). All of them touch the points at distance 1 along each axis. L∞ is a square, L2 a circle, L1 a diamond.

q: Why shouldn't you use Lp distance on (height in inches, weight in lbs, income in $)?
a: Units differ, so one coordinate can dominate
w: Lp distances can't handle three dimensions
Lp distances only work on integer values
Incomes can be negative, which breaks Lp
e: Coordinates with different units let one (e.g., income) dominate, and changing units changes the result. Normalizing to [0,1] or to mean/variance are 'hacks, not solutions'. Otherwise you're 'comparing apples to oranges'.

q: Mahalanobis distance d_M(a,b) = √((a−b)ᵀM(a−b)) reduces to Euclidean distance when:
w: M is diagonal with negative entries
e: M skews space. It's a metric when M is positive definite (all eigenvalues positive and real).

q: Cosine distance is d_cos(a,b) = ?
e: It only cares about direction, not magnitude.

q: Why is cosine distance only a pseudometric?
a: a and 2a have distance 0 but differ
w: It isn't symmetric in a and b
e: a and 2a have distance 0 but aren't equal (M2 fails); the triangle inequality also fails. Angular distance arccos(⟨a,b⟩) on normalized vectors is a true metric (a geodesic on the sphere).

q: The LSH function for cosine distance with random vector v is:
w: The minimum hash over a's set
e: It records which side of a random hyperplane a falls on. v ∈ {−1,+1}ᵈ is sufficient.

q: Jaccard distance d_J(A,B) equals:
e: 1 − |A∩B| / |A∪B|  (equivalently |AΔB| / |A∪B|). It's a true metric. The symmetric-difference form helps prove the triangle inequality.

q: Which metric properties does KL divergence violate?
w: None of them; it's a true metric
e: d_KL(P‖Q) = Σ pᵢ ln(pᵢ/qᵢ) = H(P,Q) − H(P): extra bits to express P given knowledge of Q.

q: Edit distance (insert/delete only) between 'mines' and 'smiles' is:
e: Insert s → smines, delete n → smies, insert l → smiles.

q: Why is edit distance poor for large text documents?
a: It's slow and too sensitive to small edits
w: It isn't actually a metric on strings
It only works on numeric data like vectors
It always evaluates to 0 for long documents
e: It's slow, and removing one sentence can create a large distance without changing meaning. It's great for short strings like spelling correction. An edit distance > 3 is already 'pretty large'.

q: Hop distance between two vertices in an undirected graph is:
a: The fewest edges on a path between them
w: The number of vertices in the whole graph
The total weight of every connecting path
The degree of the starting vertex
e: It's a metric. A shortcut through c would contradict 'shortest', which gives the triangle inequality.

q: What's the key idea for answering 'which items are near query q?' without checking all n items?
e: Pre-computation: build a data structure D_P on the dataset first. Then queries like D_P(q, r) or nearest neighbor φ_P(q) can be answered fast.

q: Nearest neighbor in 1 dimension takes about log n time using:
e: A balanced binary tree (or a B-tree for cache efficiency). In a B-tree, each node splits into B pieces, where B is the cache block size.

q: Why aren't Voronoi diagrams used for exact NN in high dimensions?
a: Their complexity grows exponentially in d
w: They never give exact nearest neighbors
They only work for one-dimensional data
e: Their complexity can grow as Θ(n^⌈d/2⌉), exponential in d. In d = 2 or 3 they give about log n query time.

q: p is an ε-approximate nearest neighbor of q if:
w: p is within ε of every point
e: Since distance is a modeling choice, returning any 'close enough' point is often fine, and much faster.

q: A kd-tree splits boxes by:
w: Into 2ᵈ equal pieces around the center
Along random hyperplanes at each level
e: Alternating dimensions, splitting at the median point (so it's balanced, log₂ n levels, size 2n). Quad-trees split into 2ᵈ boxes at the geometric center. R-trees use possibly-overlapping rectangles.

q: Which structure do most algorithms with theoretical guarantees use (O(log n) leaf finding, O(n) size)?
e: R-trees adapt well in practice but lack strong guarantees.

q: In hierarchical ANN search, a sibling box Bᵢ can be skipped when:
a: Its min distance to q is ≥ τ/(1+ε)
w: It contains more than 10 data points
It is larger than the current leaf box
It sits at the root of the tree
e: min distance from q to Bᵢ ≥ τ/(1+ε), where τ is the current best distance. No point inside could be a sufficiently better neighbor.

q: As d → ∞, the volume of the unit ball ____ while the unit cube (side 2) ____.
e: Box-based search returns everything in the box when you want the ball, and the gap explodes.

q: What's the basic problem with nearest neighbors in high dimensions (d > 12)?
a: Almost all distances look about the same
e: In random data in a cube or ball, most points are about the same distance apart.

q: Clustering kd-trees (David Lowe, inventor of SIFT) split each node using:
e: A 2-means clustering, putting each cluster in one subtree. It worked very well in ℝ¹²⁸. Like random-rotation kd-trees, it adapts to the data's intrinsic dimension.

q: For 2-approximate NN, LSH query time is roughly O(n^ρ) with ρ = ?
e: For n = 10 billion, n^(1/7) ≈ 10. Storage is roughly O(n^(1+ρ)).

q: LSH is theoretically optimal in high dimensions, but in practice:
a: It tends to lose to graph methods like HNSW
w: It is always the fastest method available
It can't actually be implemented efficiently
It requires labeled data for every query
e: It tends to work less well than graph-based approaches like HNSW. FALCONN is a well-engineered LSH library.

q: In basic neighborhood-graph search, when do you stop?
a: When no neighbor is closer to q
w: When you reach a leaf node
When every point has been visited
e: When no neighbor of the current point is closer to q than the current point. It's a greedy 'graph gradient descent' over the k-NN graph.

q: Beam search improves graph search by:
w: Keeping only one candidate per step
e: Keeping K > 1 candidates at each step, making it robust to local minima. Even K = 5 dramatically improves results with little overhead.

q: What does the 'hierarchical' part of HNSW provide?
a: Long-range links up top, local links at the bottom
w: Exact answers guaranteed at every single layer
A separate Voronoi diagram for each of the layers
Random hashing at each level instead of edges
e: Top layers with diverse, long-range links for fast early movement; a k-NN graph at the bottom for local convergence. It's like a generalized skip list, with a constant number of steps per layer.

q: FAISS speeds up graph-based ANN on GPUs using:
e: Quantization (a vector compression trick). Other libraries: hnswlib, DiskANN, and Pinecone's write-ups.
